![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226023/assets/f62e6a4cec5b2a877f2491a101f3929edd6664424b86daab4bbfe8096c5c9282.png)

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve $r=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\theta ),$ represented by the shaded region shown above?
question.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\theta )$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{cos}^{2}⁡(5\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits. 

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
3\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\theta )=0.
$$

Notice that the first petal lies between the first and fourth quadrants. So it's convenient to assume that $\theta $ can be negative.

We now solve the above equation for $5\theta \in [-\pi ,\pi ):$

$$
5\theta =-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,\theta =-\frac{\pi }{10},\frac{\pi }{10}
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for $\theta \in [-\frac{\pi }{10},\frac{\pi }{10}].$ Notice that this interval lies between the first and fourth quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /10}^{\pi /10}{cos}^{2}⁡(5\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$
